• Nvidia-backed AI data-center operator Firmus withdrew its application to list on the Australian Securities Exchange on October 9, scrapping a deal priced at A$11 a share targeting a roughly A$44 billion valuation.
  • The IPO would have been Australia's biggest listing since Telstra's 1997 privatization — and the world's fourth-largest this year, behind SpaceX, CXMT and Cerebras, per Dealogic data.
  • Firmus's board said the terms available “would not appropriately reflect the strength of the business”; the company will pursue private-market capital instead.
  • The collapse rattled Australian markets: construction partner Maas Group entered a trading halt after its shares plunged more than 20% on reports the listing was in trouble.

The biggest listing that wasn't

Firmus Grid, the Nvidia-backed cloud-computing company building AI data centers in Australia, has scrapped plans for what would have been the country's largest initial public offering in nearly three decades. The seven-year-old company said Friday it had withdrawn its application to list on the Australian Securities Exchange, citing “recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions.”

https://youtube.com/watch?v=RHRM6nbujO8

The numbers explain why the deal mattered. Firmus had been looking to raise almost US$5 billion at a market capitalization of more than US$30 billion, with shares priced at A$11 apiece for a valuation near A$44 billion, according to ABC News and Bloomberg. Trading had been penciled in for later this month. It will not happen.

“The board determined that the terms on which the offer could proceed would not appropriately reflect the strength of the company's business and long-term growth outlook,” Firmus said in a statement. “Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options.”

Why investors balked

The official explanation — market volatility — tells only part of the story. Bloomberg reported on October 8 that Firmus had already shut its bookbuilding process as investor support faltered, days after the company had been cutting its IPO price to keep the deal alive. This time it did not reprice or delay. It walked away.

Prospective investors told Reuters they were uneasy about three things: a valuation that had ballooned from roughly US$1 billion a year ago, the company's ability to deliver on ambitious expansion plans, and its heavy debt load. Investor documents seen by Bloomberg show Firmus has a pipeline of 912 megawatts of data-center capacity — of which only 46 megawatts has actually been built. The company sells ready-to-use computing power to large tech firms including OpenAI, its anchor customer, and Meta, and counts Blackstone and Coatue Management among its backers, with a US$10 billion Blackstone-led debt facility already in place.

“I've never seen an IPO so polarizing. There was a lot of international investor interest, however, when it comes to the crunch, the demand seems like it isn't there when they were asked to put up the capital.”

— Jun Bei Liu, Ten Cap Investment, on Bloomberg TV

The company began life in 2019 as a Bitcoin mining operation before reinventing itself as a builder of modular “AI factories” running on Nvidia hardware and proprietary cooling technology — a transformation that rode the artificial-intelligence boom to one of the most hyped listings of the year.

The market fallout

The withdrawal landed hard in Sydney. Shares of Maas Group, a construction services provider that pledged an additional A$300 million to Firmus in August (lifting its stake to 3.2%), entered a trading halt on Friday pending an announcement about its contractual arrangements with the data-center operator. The halt followed a brutal Thursday session in which Maas shares plunged more than 20%, erasing about A$517 million in market value and leaving the stock down over 30% from its record high earlier this month.

Investors called the collapse a blow to Australia's already shrinking share market. Just US$1.37 billion in new share sales priced in Australia in the first nine months of 2026, per LSEG data — the most since 2021, but dwarfed by rival exchanges. Hong Kong alone saw 118 companies raise around US$50 billion via IPOs in the same period.

A warning sign for the AI boom

The Firmus failure is the clearest signal yet that investor appetite for AI-linked listings is becoming selective, even as the AI boom powers global equity markets. Last month, smart-ring maker Oura suspended its Nasdaq listing plans, citing IPO-market uncertainty. Analysts point to surging bond yields, rising global interest rates and broader macroeconomic uncertainty as the headwinds.

For now, Firmus is in talks with existing and new investors about a private funding round — a path that avoids public-market scrutiny but keeps the company's enormous capital needs front and center. Whether private backers will pay what public investors would not is the next test of just how durable the AI-infrastructure trade really is.

• Chef Siddharth Parab, executive chef at SpiceKlub USA in Cupertino, California, says authenticity in Indian cuisine means respecting flavours and methods — not freezing recipes in time.
  • In his kitchens, modern tools like sous-vide, foams and spherification are used to “enhance, not replace” traditional taste: a deconstructed pani puri still carries the familiar punch of mint and tamarind.
  • His view echoes a wider industry shift toward hyper-regional Indian cooking, where diners reward dishes tied to a specific place and story over generic, one-menu-fits-all fare.
  • For diners: look past the theatrics when you eat Indian food in the US — a menu that names its region and keeps classic spice work intact is the real test of the authenticity Parab describes.

In a conversation with the Hindustan Times, chef Siddharth Parab offered a working definition of authenticity. Authenticity, he argues, lives in flavour and technique — in the spice work, the souring agent, the texture a dish is meant to have — not in rigid rules about how a dish must look, where it may be cooked, or whether the kitchen owns a liquid-nitrogen tank.

Parab speaks from an unusual vantage point. As executive chef at SpiceKlub USA in Cupertino, he leads a kitchen that reimagines Indian street food through molecular gastronomy for American diners — the very kind of restaurant where the authenticity question comes up most often.

“Enhance, not replace”

Parab's formula is disarmingly simple. Modern techniques are tools for presentation and texture, never substitutes for flavour. A chutney can become a foam; a curry can be encapsulated in a sphere. What cannot change is the taste a diner expects when they bite in. “We might turn a chutney into a foam or encapsulate a curry, but the taste remains familiar,” he has said in interviews describing his kitchen's philosophy.

“Balancing innovation with authenticity starts with respect for the traditional flavours and methods that define Indian cuisine.”

— Chef Siddharth Parab

The example he returns to is telling: a deconstructed pani puri may look nothing like the crisp puri served at a Mumbai chaat stall, but it must still carry the unmistakable sour-sweet hit of mint and tamarind. Get that wrong and no amount of technical theatre saves the dish; get it right and the new form becomes a way of honouring the old one. The dividing line, in his words, is that “while the presentation might be modern, the soul of the dish — its flavours and essence — stays rooted in tradition.”

Precision matters here. Parab stresses careful spicing and cultural sensibility — the understanding that a dish carries the memory of the community that made it. That is what separates respectful reinvention from novelty for its own sake.

A wider shift toward regional roots

Parab's argument lands at a moment when Indian fine dining is having the same conversation with itself. Across the industry, chefs are moving past the familiar greatest-hits menus of butter chicken and biryani toward hyper-regional cooking — dishes defined by a specific locality, community and ingredient, from Malnad pork curry to Kodava bamboo-shoot preparations. Research from the National Restaurant Association of India has found diners increasingly valuing genuine regional cooking, quality ingredients and stories behind dishes over mere familiarity.

The change is visible on both sides of the ocean. In India, restaurants are retracing cultural roots and putting once-dismissed home dishes on premium menus. In the US, menus are widening beyond the old North Indian staples to regional breads, fermented batters and pickles that would have been unthinkable a decade ago.

Why it matters for the diaspora table

For Indian-American diners, the stakes are personal. Diaspora families have long faced two unsatisfying choices when eating out: the museum-piece restaurant that treats Indian food as a relic, or the adapted version that sands down the sour, the bitter and the funky to suit a presumed Western palate. Parab's middle path — familiar flavour, modern form — offers a third option, and it is one that second-generation diners, fluent in both cultures, have been asking for.

It also matters who gets to define the cuisine. Parab's career — from Mumbai's Hyatt Regency and a stint with Michelin-starred chef Raymond Blanc in the UK to the Lodha Group and now California — mirrors the path of many diaspora chefs. His answer to the “is it real?” question is that realness was never about the props.

What's next

Parab's stated long-term goal is a flagship restaurant that fuses tradition with modern technique outright — a destination for contemporary Indian cuisine — alongside mentoring young chefs to, in his words, carry traditions forward “while innovating boldly.” If the current direction of Indian dining holds, his definition of authenticity may soon stop sounding like an argument and start sounding like the industry standard.

• On Kaun Banega Crorepati 18, Madhuri Dixit told host Amitabh Bachchan that her late mother Snehlata — whom she called “Aai” — taught her not to be weak: “just work, and work with sincerity.”
  • She said she joined films very young and criticism would hurt; her mother's advice became the framework that carried her through early failures to stardom.
  • The arc is well documented: a 1984 debut, years of flops and harsh judgment, then Tezaab (1988) and “Ek Do Teen” made her Bollywood's biggest female star — six Filmfare Awards and the Padma Shri followed.
  • For fans abroad: Madhuri is set to host the Marathi edition of the quiz format, Kon Honaar Crorepati, her first full-time hosting role — diaspora viewers should watch for streaming details.

On a recent episode of Kaun Banega Crorepati 18, Madhuri Dixit opened up to host Amitabh Bachchan about the person she credits for both her art and her resilience: her late mother, Snehlata Dixit, whom she called “Aai.”

Bachchan asked whether she had learned a great deal from the woman she calls Aai, and Dixit did not hesitate. She said her love for art and dance came from her mother, and recalled her earliest days in the industry, when she was very young and the criticism stung. Her mother's instruction, delivered in the plain Hindi of home, became her working philosophy: “Itna weak nahi hona … bas kaam karo aur sincerity se kaam karo” — don't be so weak; just work, and work with sincerity.

What “Aai” taught her

Dixit's shorthand for the lesson was even shorter: karke dikhao — show it through your work. It is advice she has cited across the decades. At a Goafest 2022 session, when she was doubting her decision to enter films, she recalled her mother telling her to “give it my all and to put in the hard work with dedication,” calling her mother an immense source of encouragement. In a 2022 interview she described being told she didn't look like a heroine — too young, too petite — and said she survived the criticism by following her mother's counsel: do good work, and recognition will follow.

“Itna weak nahi hona... bas kaam karo aur sincerity se kaam karo.”

— Madhuri Dixit, quoting her mother Snehlata on KBC 18

Snehlata Dixit died in March 2023 at the age of 90, and the KBC conversation carried the weight of that absence. Dixit has said her mother's treatment of her never changed with fame — she was still scolded for a messy room after becoming a star — and that grounding, she suggested on the show, is what kept her steady through the industry's highs and lows.

The struggle years

It is easy to forget, watching the polished icon, how rough the start was. Dixit debuted with Abodh and spent years in films that sank without a trace, enduring the industry's casual cruelty about her looks and her Maharashtrian middle-class background. Industry veterans have recalled seeing the young actress and her mother waiting outside Film City, treated as nobodies. The rejections were not abstract — they were daily, personal, and public.

What turned it around was work, exactly as her mother prescribed. Tezaab (1988) and its chart-busting number “Ek Do Teen,” choreographed by Saroj Khan, made her an overnight sensation at an age when many would have quit. The career that followed — Ram Lakhan, Dil, Beta, Hum Aapke Hain Koun..!, Dil To Pagal Hai, Devdas — brought six Filmfare Awards and the Padma Shri, and a reputation as Hindi cinema's finest dancer-actress.

A career the diaspora grew up with

Dixit's story resonates well beyond India. After marrying cardiovascular surgeon Dr. Shriram Nene, she spent years living in the United States, raising her family away from the arc lights — a chapter that made her one of the few Bollywood superstars the diaspora could claim as a neighbour.

That connection has endured through her second innings — the Netflix series The Fame Game and a steady presence on reality television — and now a move into hosting. Appearing on KBC 18 as a special guest during Bachchan's birthday week, she even turned the tables on the host, playing his “Ek Do Teen” clip from Toofan back at him.

What's next

Dixit is set to step into the host's chair herself, fronting the Marathi-language edition of the quiz format titled Kon Honaar Crorepati. It is a significant move — one of Bollywood's most recognisable faces anchoring a regional franchise — and, fittingly for an actress whose mother taught her to answer doubt with work, it is a new stage rather than a comfortable one.

• Elon Musk escalated his fight over Starlink's stalled India launch on October 8, posting on X: “Is Ambani the real boss of India?” — directly naming Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani for the first time.
  • A day earlier, Musk had accused unnamed “oligarchs” of blocking Starlink to protect a “monopolistic chokehold,” calling the delay “a crime against the people of India.”
  • India's Ministry of Communications rejected the charge, saying its satellite-communications framework is “fair and non-discriminatory” and that Starlink is at the same regulatory stage as two other licensed operators.
  • Anyone in India waiting for satellite broadband will have to keep waiting: Starlink must still complete security assessments before it can even seek spectrum, and no launch date has been set.

From “oligarchs” to Ambani by name

Elon Musk's long-running frustration with India's regulators turned personal this week. On Wednesday, the SpaceX founder accused unnamed “oligarchs” of blocking Starlink's satellite-internet launch in India to maintain what he called their “monopolistic chokehold” on the country, without naming names or offering evidence. “You can guess who they are,” he added in a follow-up post.

https://x.com/TimesNow/status/2108261167991009402

On Thursday, he named the name. “Starlink is licensed in over 165 countries and has spent five years complying with every single law and requirement of the government of India, so why still no license?” Musk wrote on X. “Is Ambani the real boss of India?”

“Starlink is licensed in over 165 countries and has spent five years complying with every single law and requirement of the government of India, so why still no license? Is Ambani the real boss of India?”

— Elon Musk, on X, October 8

The remark was aimed squarely at Mukesh Ambani, whose telecom arm Reliance Jio — with more than 500 million subscribers — dominates Indian connectivity. Musk has argued that Starlink could bring affordable high-speed internet to Indians who lack access, and he called the alleged blocking “a crime against the people of India.”

New Delhi pushes back

Hours after Musk's initial posts, India's Ministry of Communications issued a pointed rebuttal. The ministry said its regulatory framework for satellite communications is “fair and non-discriminatory,” and that Starlink and two other licensed satellite operators are all at “broadly the same regulatory stage.” All three companies, it added, are undergoing security assessments that must be completed before they can seek spectrum — the radio frequencies satellites use to transmit signals.

A minister went further in comments to NDTV, declaring that “India doesn't allow monopoly in any sector” — a direct answer to Musk's claim of a protected incumbent chokehold.

Five years of waiting

Starlink's India story has been one of the longest-running sagas in global telecom. The company has spent more than five years trying to enter a market with over a billion internet subscribers, yet has never begun commercial service there. Along the way it secured key regulatory approvals and — ironically, given this week's rhetoric — struck distribution partnerships with both Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel last year. SpaceX also set up a local team, appointing former Payoneer executive Prabhakar Jayakumar to lead its India operations in December.

India's telecom market is among the most concentrated in the world: Jio and Airtel together hold more than 80% of the market. Jio has been widely credited with slashing mobile-data prices since its launch a decade ago — the very affordability argument Musk is now making for satellite. And Ambani's camp is not standing still: in June, Akash Ambani told Jio shareholders the company plans to roll out low-orbit satellite communications by leasing capacity from global constellation providers, putting it on a direct collision course with Starlink.

Musk's broadside drew a cheeky response from opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, who replied “Welcome to India.” Musk answered with a “thank you.”

What's at stake

The immediate question is regulatory, not rhetorical. Until Starlink clears India's security assessments and receives spectrum, the license Musk is demanding cannot be issued — and New Delhi has shown no sign of accelerating the process in response to pressure. SpaceX's Starlink chief Lauren Dreyer noted at the India Mobile Congress this week that the network now has some 11,000 satellites in orbit serving more than 170 countries. India remains the conspicuous exception.

For the Indian diaspora, the fight is more than a billionaire feud. Millions of NRIs have family in rural and remote parts of India where ground networks are thin or unreliable — precisely the areas satellite internet is built to serve. A Starlink launch could reshape connectivity for those households, and sharpen price competition that has already transformed Indian telecom once. For now, though, the war of words is the only thing moving faster than the satellites: the launch timeline remains blank, and the Jio partnership Musk once touted now looks distinctly frosty.

• Russian President Vladimir Putin met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan on October 8, ahead of Friday's Commonwealth of Independent States summit at the Caspian Sea resort of Avaza.
  • Putin said Russia is “ready to do everything that is in our power” to help bring an end to the Middle East war that began with US-Israeli attacks on Iran on February 28.
  • He credited Iran with making “real efforts” to end the conflict and noted the “positive evolution” of Moscow-Tehran relations.
  • Russia has announced no specific peace plan or timetable — the offer is diplomatic positioning for now, as Trump separately claims “productive discussions” with Tehran.

The meeting in Turkmenistan

Russian President Vladimir Putin told Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Thursday that Moscow stands ready to help end the war in the Middle East, placing Russia more visibly at the center of diplomacy around the months-long conflict.

“We are ready to do everything that is in our power to contribute to the settlement of this situation,” Putin said, according to Russian state media, as the two leaders met in Turkmenistan ahead of a Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) summit that opens Friday in the Caspian resort town of Avaza.

“We are ready to do everything that is in our power to contribute to the settlement of this situation.”

— Vladimir Putin, meeting Masoud Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan

Putin added that Iran had made “real efforts to end the war” since the conflict began on February 28, when the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran, according to Russian news agencies. He also pointed to “positive developments” in relations between the two countries.

An alliance deepened by sanctions

The optics of the meeting were as important as the words. Russia and Iran — two of the world's most heavily sanctioned nations — have significantly deepened their military and trade ties since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, becoming increasingly reliant on each other. Thursday's encounter, held on the sidelines of a gathering of former Soviet republics, underscored how that partnership has matured into open political coordination.

Moscow's alignment with Tehran over the war is explicit: Putin framed the conflict as one that had not begun through Iran's own actions, echoing the Kremlin's longstanding line. Russia has previously offered to help stabilize the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf region — a strategically vital waterway that Iran continues to restrict as the conflict grinds on.

Why Moscow wants a seat at the table

Putin's offer arrives as diplomatic traffic around the conflict intensifies. Earlier this year, during a phone call with US President Donald Trump, Putin reportedly proposed that Russia take custody of Iran's enriched uranium as part of a broader deal to end the war — an offer Trump declined, telling Putin: “Before you help me, I want to end your war,” in reference to Ukraine.

Trump, meanwhile, has been touting what he calls “productive discussions” with Tehran, according to Fox News — suggesting parallel, competing mediation tracks between Washington and Moscow. Russia's repeated high-level contact with Pezeshkian signals that the Kremlin wants a guaranteed role in any eventual settlement, even as it maintains its strategic relationship with Tehran.

What to watch

For now, Russia's pledge remains diplomatic rather than operational: no peace plan, no timetable, and no announced mechanism for mediation. The substance will be tested at the CIS summit on Friday and in whether Moscow follows words with concrete proposals.

For Indian readers, the stakes are tangible even at a distance. The war has kept energy markets volatile and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz constrained for months — pressures that feed directly into fuel prices and inflation back home. A credible mediation track, whether Russian, American, or joint, would be the first sign in months that the conflict's economic drag on the region might finally ease.

• Oxford Area High School in Chester County, Pennsylvania, is closed to all students and staff on Friday, Oct. 9, after a measles case was confirmed in connection with the campus community, the district announced late Thursday.
  • The one-day closure gives officials time to audit and verify measles immunity records for every staff member in the high school building — a step mandated by the Chester County Health Department — while crews run enhanced cleaning.
  • County health officials are leading contact tracing and will notify anyone with direct exposure. Unvaccinated students or staff, or anyone unable to prove immunity, must stay out of school and school functions for 21 days.
  • What families should do now: locate your child's immunization records, and watch for guidance from the Chester County Health Department and the Pennsylvania Department of Health.

Oxford Area High School in Chester County, Pennsylvania, closed its doors to all students and staff on Friday, Oct. 9, after a measles case was confirmed in connection with the campus community, the Oxford Area School District announced late Thursday.

Superintendent David A. Woods informed families in an official letter, according to Fox29, saying the temporary closure would give administrators time to audit and verify measles immunity records for every staff member working inside the high school building. That review is a protocol mandated by the Chester County Health Department (CCHD).

"The health and well-being of our students, staff and community are incredibly important to us, and we recognize that receiving this information can raise questions, concerns and uncertainty."

— David A. Woods, Superintendent, Oxford Area School District

A one-day pause for records and cleaning

The district framed the closure as a logistical step, not an extended shutdown. While the building sits empty, maintenance crews will carry out enhanced cleaning and sanitization throughout the facility.

Public health officials from CCHD are leading the contact-tracing effort and will directly notify anyone determined to have had direct exposure to the infected person, Woods wrote. The district's statement said anyone not vaccinated for measles, or unable to prove vaccination, cannot attend school or school functions and must quarantine for 21 days — matching Pennsylvania's standing exclusion policy for measles exposure.

Woods acknowledged the anxiety such news creates for parents. "We understand that news like this may be concerning for families," he wrote, adding that the district is "committed to keeping our school community informed, supporting our families and working in partnership with public health officials."

A statewide outbreak as backdrop

The Oxford Area case lands in the middle of Pennsylvania's largest measles outbreak since the disease was declared eliminated in the United States. Reporting this week put the statewide count above 1,000 cases, with the Pennsylvania Department of Health recording 977 cases across 39 counties as of last Friday.

The outbreak's profile is unusual: the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy reported that 69 percent of Pennsylvania cases involve adults — the near-reverse of the national pattern.

The virus is reaching school-age settings elsewhere in the state too. A second measles case was confirmed in Allegheny County this week, according to Pittsburgh outlets WPXI and Public Source, and several western Pennsylvania districts have drafted response plans built on the same three tools: isolation, disinfection, and 21-day exclusions for the unvaccinated, the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette reported.

What it means for families

For parents, the immediate consequence is a single day of closure — but the longer shadow is the exclusion rule. Any student or staff member who cannot document measles immunity could be kept out of school and school activities for three weeks if exposure is confirmed, regardless of whether the school reopens on schedule.

The practical step is to find vaccination records now rather than during a tracing call. Families who cannot locate their child's records should contact their pediatrician or family doctor; Pennsylvania's school vaccination requirements mean most students should already have documentation on file with the school nurse's office.

Health officials also urge families to watch for measles symptoms — high fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes, and a characteristic rash — and to call a doctor before visiting a clinic if symptoms appear, so exposure to others can be limited.

What happens next

The district has announced no closure beyond Friday. The next moves belong to the Chester County Health Department: its contact tracers will work through the exposure list over the coming days, and anyone identified as directly exposed will be notified and given exclusion instructions.

If additional cases emerge, the exclusion window extends — unimmunized contacts stay out until 21 days after the last case's onset.

For the broader region, the Oxford closure signals that Pennsylvania's record outbreak is reaching into school buildings, and other districts will likely follow the same playbook: rapid closures for record audits, contact tracing, and strict proof-of-immunity enforcement.

• Google Maps' first Fan-Favourite Dining List reports a 136% year-on-year rise in Seattle reviews mentioning dosas — one of the biggest single-dish surges on the list.
  • The list, built from reviews, ratings and aggregated direction requests across 10 world cities between September 2025 and August 2026, names Shri Ananda Bhavan and Chennai Express as Seattle's dosa hotspots.
  • Other findings: frozen yoghurt is back in New York (up 320%), mochi is surging in Tokyo (up 168%), and matcha keeps climbing across nearly all 10 cities.
  • Planning a Seattle trip? The full interactive list is live at mapsfanfavorites.withgoogle.com — search the Seattle tab for dosa spots near you.

In India, the dosa hardly needs an introduction: the crisp, fermented rice-and-lentil crepe is a breakfast staple and a comfort order at every South Indian restaurant. What it apparently needed was an introduction to Seattle — and judging by new Google Maps data, the two have now met. Reviews mentioning “dosas” in the US city rose 136% year-on-year, making the humble South Indian dish one of the standout food trends in Google's first-ever Fan-Favourite Dining List.

The list, announced this week, is Google's first dining guide built on real-world behaviour: reviews, ratings and aggregated requests for directions, gathered across 10 cities deemed global hot spots — Atlanta, Chicago, London, Melbourne, Montreal, New York, San Francisco, Santiago, Seattle and Tokyo. A live hub at mapsfanfavorites.withgoogle.com lets users browse each city by essentials, occasions and items trending in reviews.

What the numbers show

The 2026 list draws on Google Maps data from September 2025 through August 2026, including reviews and ratings from the Local Guides community, aggregated searches for directions and a final verification pass. Dosa's 136% jump in Seattle sits among the sharpest single-item surges in the report: for comparison, frozen yoghurt mentions rose 320% in New York, mochi mentions 168% in Tokyo, cinnamon buns 84% in Montreal, hojicha 114% in London and ube 75% in Melbourne. Matcha kept climbing in nearly every city, with Chicago up 82% and Santiago 84%.

https://x.com/Google/status/2108204734469324976

“Our first-ever Fan-Favorite list spotlights top local restaurants and culinary trends across 10 cities — made possible only by Google Maps and the billions of people who use it to find, review, and rate places to eat.”

— Andrew Duchi, director of product management at Google

In Seattle, the report points dosa hunters toward Shri Ananda Bhavan and Chennai Express — two names familiar to anyone who has asked a South Indian in the Emerald City where to eat. The data does not say exactly what is driving the surge, but the likeliest explanation is the simplest: more people tried it, more people wrote about it, and the city's growing appetite did the rest.

Why dosa, why Seattle

Seattle is, in many ways, an obvious place for this to happen. The city's tech corridor — home to large Amazon and Microsoft workforces — has one of the densest South Indian diaspora populations in the United States, and its Indian restaurant scene has quietly deepened over the past decade. What was once a landscape of generic curry houses now includes dedicated South Indian kitchens, Kerala specialists and dosa-focused counters, giving newcomers and the merely curious plenty of on-ramps.

The dosa itself helps. Naturally gluten-free, customisable, and vegetarian-friendly, it fits neatly into the dietary Venn diagram of the Pacific Northwest — and its theatre, the dramatic spread of batter on a screaming-hot griddle, makes it one of the most photogenic dishes in Indian cuisine. In a ranking built partly on what people photograph, review and rave about, that matters.

The diaspora angle

For Indian-Americans, there is something quietly satisfying about watching a dish their grandmothers made on Sunday mornings show up in a Google trend report alongside froyo and beignets. Indian food's American journey — from the butter-chicken era of the 1990s to today's regional specificity — has been driven in large part by the diaspora itself: the restaurants families opened, the lunchboxes colleagues got curious about, the second-generation food writers who insisted there was more to the cuisine than the greatest-hits menu.

A 136% jump in review mentions is, strictly speaking, a measure of chatter rather than consumption. But chatter is how food trends start, and for a dish that spent decades as an insider order, being Seattle's most talked-about bite is a milestone worth noting. Pass the sambar.

• A 2025 EY analysis attributes a 20–25% cut in entry-level IT hiring in India to automation, according to reports; a Nomura survey found 55% of Indian IT firms reduced entry-level hiring, against just 14% for senior roles.
  • Global capability centres are also under pressure: estimates put job cuts at 5,000 to 30,000 this fiscal year, with Cambium Networks shutting its Bengaluru centre in October (around 200 employees) and Hy-Vee closing its India engineering centre in June (around 150), per BusinessLine.
  • An Indeed survey found 70% of young Indians say landing a first job is harder than it was three to five years ago, with 72% saying employers expect prior experience even for entry-level roles and 61% rarely getting a response after applying.
  • What helps: recruiters now prioritise AI, data and cloud skills over degrees (64%, per the Unstop Talent Report 2026); routine testing, basic coding and QA roles are the ones being automated; freshers improve their odds with demonstrated AI fluency, real project portfolios, paid internships, and targeting GCCs, semiconductors and consulting firms, which are still hiring.

The degree is done. The job is not. Across India, a growing number of graduates are discovering that the old contract — study hard, earn a degree, get absorbed by a hiring engine — is breaking down at exactly the point it used to hold: the entry-level job. A 2025 analysis by EY attributed a 20–25% cut in entry-level hiring in India to automation, and the class of 2026 is walking into the aftermath.

The squeeze is not just an IT story, but IT is where it bites hardest. Automation is swallowing the exact tasks that used to be a fresher's first two or three years of work: fixing small bugs, writing test cases, triaging tickets, resolving routine customer queries. India Today reports that students are struggling to land entry-level roles as automation takes over — and the data behind that headline is stark.

What's changing: the bottom rung is being pulled away

Start with the numbers. According to reports on the EY analysis, entry-level IT roles are down 20–25% because of automation. Nomura found 55% of Indian IT firms reduced entry-level hiring, compared with just 14% for senior roles. Stanford researchers found employment for 22–25-year-olds in AI-exposed fields down 13% since generative AI went mainstream.

The Times of India, citing a World Bank report, frames the same shift in white-collar hiring: generative AI has begun hitting entry-level hiring in India as demand for AI skills rises, with job postings declining significantly for roles where AI can serve as a substitute — even as new roles such as AI ethics specialists emerge.

The hiring collapse is visible in the industry's own figures. Staffing data cited in recent reports shows net IT hiring sliding from around 6 lakh in FY22 to roughly 1.4 lakh in FY26. CLSA data shows freshers account for just 13% of active tech openings, and Infosys's share of employees under 30 fell from 60% to 51% in three years. Meanwhile NASSCOM pegs the tech sector at $315 billion in FY26, up 6.1%, with about 135,000 net new jobs — revenue and headcount, once joined at the hip, have quietly separated.

GCCs feel the squeeze too

The global capability centres — long pitched as the new, higher-value absorber of Indian engineering talent — are not immune. BusinessLine reports a string of layoffs and closures: Cambium Networks shut its Bengaluru GCC in October, affecting around 200 employees, and Hy-Vee closed its India engineering centre in June, impacting around 150. Reported reductions also include roughly 200 jobs at PayPal, about 1,500 roles at Visa, and cuts at ServiceNow.

“If the leadership doesn't view the India center as an IP creation or innovation center, there may be full-fledged shutdowns.”

— Gaurav Vasu, CEO and founder of UnearthInsight, quoted by BusinessLine

Industry estimates for GCC job cuts this fiscal year range widely, from around 5,000 to as many as 30,000 roles, against a workforce of 2.4–2.5 million professionals across more than 2,100 centres. Alouk Kumar, founder and CEO of Inductus Group, told BusinessLine that parent-company restructuring and global cost-cutting account for an estimated 50–60% of GCC layoffs, AI-led productivity gains for another 15–20%, and GCC-specific portfolio weakness for 10–15%. Gaurav Vasu estimates more than 400 GCCs could remain under stress over the next few years. Even so, GCCs continue to be the biggest driver of tech hiring in India and could generate around 150,000 new jobs this fiscal year — just not the same kinds of jobs.

The student experience: qualified, experienced — and ignored

An Indeed survey of young Indians puts numbers to the frustration. Seventy percent believe securing a first job is significantly harder than three to five years ago; 72% say employers expect prior experience even for entry-level roles; 61% say they rarely receive a response after applying. The “experience contradiction” — employers wanting candidates who can hit the ground running, from graduates who have never run — is the defining feature of the current market.

The Unstop Talent Report 2026, based on more than 37,000 students and 500 HR leaders, found 85% of engineering students and 84% of undergraduates still unplaced even though 87.8% of HR leaders say they are actively hiring. Only 40% of freshers secure salaries above ₹5 lakh per annum, while 73% expect it. Only 20% of respondents secured a paid internship during their studies, and 43% say financial constraints are limiting their options. Sixty-four percent say repeated rejection has eroded their self-confidence or motivation.

Colleges are adapting on the fly. The National Institute of Technology, Jamshedpur, capped campus recruiter participation at a minimum ₹6 lakh package, since IT firms typically hire in bulk at ₹3.5–4 lakh, professor Saroj Kumar Sarangi told Mint — and he expects GCCs to pick up graduates for skill-based roles, particularly in AI, rather than the traditional software developer positions.

The diaspora angle: the squeeze follows Indian students abroad

The same pressure tracks Indian students overseas. In the US, the Department of Homeland Security has proposed charging international students $70,000 for Optional Practical Training — the work authorization that serves as the bridge from a US degree to a skilled job — up from roughly $500 today, according to Reuters reporting on the proposal, which is now in a 30-day public-comment period. Around 1.44 lakh Indian students participate in OPT, per the Times of India, and Indian student enrolment in the US reportedly fell about 15% in the 2025–26 cycle, according to the Hindu. For families spending lakhs on a US education, the entry-level squeeze at home is increasingly paired with a policy squeeze abroad.

What's next

The jobs are not disappearing so much as mutating. LinkedIn's Grad's Guide 2026 found entry-level hiring in India rose 168% between 2023 and 2025, driven by AI roles, internships and hiring beyond the metros; Naukri recorded fresher hiring up 17% year-on-year in February 2026. The Bernstein equity-research firm wrote to Prime Minister Modi earlier this year warning of an employment crisis as AI threatens white-collar IT jobs — and noted India could need nearly 1 million AI-skilled professionals by 2026, with a large deficit against that number.

“The bottom rung hasn't disappeared. It moved up a few inches and got slipperier. Freshers who climb with judgement and AI fluency will be fine.”

— Abhishek Bartakke, Founder & CEO of Syncro1

The message from recruiters is consistent: stop racing the machine on speed. Compete on judgement, communication and problem framing; build a portfolio that outranks a CGPA; show AI work visibly — how you prompt, verify and improve its output. The old deal — degree in, job out — is gone. The new one is narrower, and it has AI fluency as the gatekeeper.

• The Vvaan has grossed an estimated ₹85.61 crore worldwide through 13 days — ₹66.31 crore net in India plus ₹7.35 crore overseas — according to trade estimates compiled by Koimoi.
  • The film is now Sidharth Malhotra's sixth-highest-grossing film globally, having overtaken Marjaavaan (₹65.34 crore), and is within striking distance of Param Sundari (₹89.72 crore), the next title above it on his career chart.

A steady run into the third week

The Vvaan: Force of the Forest, the folklore fantasy thriller starring Sidharth Malhotra and Tamannaah Bhatia, is holding its ground at the box office well into its third week. According to trade estimates compiled by Koimoi, the film earned ₹85.61 crore in worldwide gross through its 13th day — ₹66.31 crore net (₹78.26 crore gross) at the Indian box office, supplemented by ₹7.35 crore from overseas territories.

The day-wise pattern tells the story of a film carried by a strong opening weekend and an unusually resilient heartland audience. The film opened on September 25 to roughly ₹8 crore on day one, jumped to ₹11.25 crore on Saturday and ₹14 crore on Sunday, for a ₹33.25-crore opening weekend, per Sacnilk figures reported by iDiva. Trade analyst Taran Adarsh flagged the surge at the time, writing that mass pockets and the Hindi heartland had delivered “excellent business.”

Weekday holds in the second week were modest — day 10 brought ₹3.25 crore net, day 11 just ₹0.95 crore — but the film kept screens alive even as new competition arrived, including an Avengers: Endgame re-release and The Paradise.

Climbing Malhotra's career chart

The run has quietly become one of the more notable commercial stories of Malhotra's career. Per Koimoi's published career chart, the actor's all-time worldwide leaders are Ek Villain (₹169.62 crore), Kapoor & Sons (₹147.94 crore), Brothers (₹140.3 crore), Student of the Year (₹109.1 crore) and Param Sundari (₹89.72 crore). The Vvaan has already passed Marjaavaan, Hasee Toh Phasee and Baar Baar Dekho to sit at No. 6 — and Koimoi's latest update puts it less than ₹3 crore from overtaking Param Sundari for the No. 5 spot.

“The Vvaan takes a big step forward, hitting double digits on Saturday, with the mass pockets and heartland delivering excellent business.”

— Taran Adarsh, trade analyst

The film is also a banner milestone: Koimoi reports it is the fourth-highest-grossing venture ever for Balaji Motion Pictures, the studio that produced it jointly with TVF Motion Pictures. For Tamannaah Bhatia, the film has become her second-highest-grossing Bollywood project, according to Zoom TV.

The Chhath factor

One of the more unusual threads in the film's run is geography. Pinkvilla reported that advance sales in Bihar — a circuit whose exhibition infrastructure has thinned dramatically over the years — were running ahead of Delhi and Mumbai, something the trade press called nearly unprecedented. The driver: the film is rooted in Chhath Puja folklore, the harvest festival that dominates Bihar's cultural calendar, and its mythology-inflected story of local legends appears to have resonated directly with that audience.

That regional strength matters commercially. As FilmiMagic noted, the film's theatrical lifetime is expected to land around ₹65–70 crore net in India — a modest figure by blockbuster standards, but a genuine success for a mid-budget folklore thriller that, as Pinkvilla observed, looked “destined to be a non-starter” a month before release.

What comes next

The immediate question is whether The Vvaan can close the roughly ₹3-crore gap to Param Sundari before screens contract further. Daily collections have tapered to the ₹0.8–1.5 crore range, so the milestone will likely need another full weekend of holds. Trade watchers at NewsDIO project a final worldwide tally in the ₹85–90 crore band, which the film has now entered.

For Malhotra, whose post-COVID theatrical record has been uneven, the film is already his second-biggest grosser of the post-pandemic era. Whether it takes the No. 5 career spot or stalls just short, The Vvaan has given both its lead star and its banner a genuine theatrical win in a year when mid-budget Hindi films have struggled to find audiences.

An ICE officer shot a man sitting in his car with a 5-year-old child in New York City on Oct. 8 — and within hours, Mayor Zohran Mamdani was on the phone with President Donald Trump, demanding an end to all ICE enforcement and trying, unsuccessfully, to free the wounded man.

The shooting in Marble Hill

Around 4 p.m. ET, federal agents surrounded a gray Honda CRV in Marble Hill. NYPD cameras caught the car backing into a parking spot as a plain-clothes federal officer approached the driver's-side window with his gun drawn; the vehicle then moved out of camera range, and the shooting itself was not recorded.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=060r9GGzrI8

At least one ICE agent fired seven rounds, Tisch said, striking the driver — Oscar Belgal, 28, of the Dominican Republic, per the NYPD — in the neck below his left ear. A 5-year-old child, believed by police to be Belgal's son, was in the car and was unharmed.

Responding NYPD officers found him handcuffed on the ground and gave aid, and rushed him to NewYork-Presbyterian Allen Hospital, where he arrived stable. The department stressed it had no involvement in the federal operation. DHS confirmed an officer fired during a "targeted enforcement operation" and said aid was immediately rendered, but did not say what led the officer to fire.

"Terrorize our communities": Mamdani's condemnation

Mamdani responded within hours. In an X post sent shortly after 11 p.m., he wrote that agents had surrounded the man and the 5-year-old before firing, called the shooting "unconscionable," and said he had called Trump to demand an end to all ICE enforcement in the city.

https://x.com/anadoluagency/status/2108467516674605177

"I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities. Get ICE out of our neighborhoods. Get ICE out of our hospitals. Get ICE off our streets. Get ICE away from our children."

— Zohran Mamdani, Mayor of New York City

At a late-night news conference near the scene — with anti-ICE protesters chanting behind him — Mamdani said: "There is no explanation for federal officers firing this many rounds into a car that has a 5-year-old in the car." He accused ICE of operating "with impunity," sowing "chaos and terror" across the country, and called the agency "rotten to its core" and one that "must be abolished."

Two hours with Trump — and a failed push for release

"For the past two hours, I've been on the phone with President Trump and Secretary Mullin negotiating the release of the man ICE agents shot," the mayor said. "Those negotiations were unsuccessful." Moments before the press conference, ICE had removed Belgal from the hospital: "ICE put the man in an unmarked vehicle and whisked him away."

Mamdani said he also demanded ICE leave the scene and halt enforcement in the city. Governor Kathy Hochul said she separately spoke with both and demanded any body-camera footage be released.

DHS defended the operation and attacked the city's policies, saying Belgal had "a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs, and weapons possession" plus alleged Trinitarios gang ties, and had been arrested by the NYPD on Dec. 7, 2023, then released days later under what it called "reckless Democrat sanctuary policies."

A neighborhood already on edge

Marble Hill has become a flashpoint. On Oct. 5, eight elected officials wrote to a Target on West 225th Street citing "increasing sightings" of ICE using its parking lot as a staging area; the company told USA Today it has "no cooperative agreements with ICE or any other immigration enforcement agency."

Thursday night, crowds gathered and clashed with law enforcement near the scene. The New York Immigrant Coalition called for an investigation and the release of body-camera footage, its president saying the shooting showed "ICE's violent tactics are a clear danger to all New Yorkers."

The shooting is the latest in a string of federal-agent shootings — at least 21 people had been shot during Trump's second term before Oct. 8, per an ABC News count, including two U.S. citizens killed in Minneapolis in January. It follows a month of open friction after Mullin criticized Hochul and Mamdani for not cooperating with federal immigration authorities.

Diaspora angle

The shooting lands hard in a borough with a large, growing South Asian community. Mamdani himself is of South Asian descent, and his framing of ICE as a threat to "our communities" speaks directly to immigrant families — including Indian, Pakistani, and Bangladeshi New Yorkers — wary of stepped-up federal enforcement in the neighborhoods and stores they use daily.

What's next

Several questions are unresolved: what led the officer to fire, whether body-camera footage exists, and Belgal's custody status after ICE removed him from the hospital. Whether the Trump-Mamdani working relationship survives the mayor's demand will be the first political test.
